## Purpose and completion criteria

Assess a switch to allow multiple group columns to a simulation to allow more than one group designation within the same simulation.

| Measure | Comparison | Acceptance criterion |
|---|---|---|
| Accounting and implementation | Existing tests | Successful unit tests |

## Overview of Design

The `group` column is intended to be abstract so that users can use it for different kinds of things. For example, it could designate ethnoracial groups, educational categories, or regions. While this is useful, users are still limited to a single group column. So, if they want a simulation that includes both regional migration and ethnoracial breakdowns, they will have a difficult time. While it is possible to hack together a set of categories for a group that are a combination of multiple groups that the user wants, this is not easy or elegant.

However, we have all the internal plumbing to allow for more than one group. Its really just another stratification dimension and we know how to handle those already. So, while it will takes some work to update the code to accept multiple group columns, it doesn't require any big underlying changes to the engine. The biggest change is to the calibration method for group weighting used for intergroup partnership, which I discuss below.

To allow for multiple groups, we have created a separate `set_groups` argument for building the model. This is a change from the program inferring groups from the `group` column. Now, users can use any name they want to identify a group column (e.g. race, region, education) and then explicitly define it as a group column with the `group()` function. The inheritance model also now belongs to this `group()` output. Users can also specify explicit categories for the group in `group` rather than in the inheritance model, but if they don't, categories will be inferred from the data. So, here is an example setup:

```r
model |>
  set_groups(
   race = group(
      categories = c("white", "black", "other"),
      ancestry = TRUE,
      inheritance = create_group_inheritance("random_parent")
    ),
   region = group(
      categories = c("NE", "MW", "S", "W"),
      ancestry = FALSE,
      inheritance = create_group_inheritance("mother")
    )
  )
```

Group exogamy parameters still live in the matching model but are now specified with a named list structure where names identify which group's exogamy is being considered. So:

```r
model |>
  set_union_formation(
    "on_demand", 
    matching = create_age_gap_matching_model(
      2, 5,
      group_exogamy = list(
        race = c("white:black" = -4, "white:other" = -2, "black:other" = -3),
        region = NA
      )
    )
  )
```

This will allow for exogamy rates between each of the three racial groups, while no exogamy will be allowed between regions.

Transition rate schedules will now apply to specific groups with the `group` argument. `'group_origin` and `group_dest` have been replaced with `origin` and `destination`. The transition rates for one group can be stratified by other groups. So, for example, you could stratify educational transitions to be different by region. Here is an example of how you would set a rate schedule for a specific group:

```r
model |>
  set_group_transition(educ_trans_rates, group = "education")
```

This would set the transition rates for the education group.

### Changes to helpers

Because of the new structure, we have removed all of the `group_prop_hazard` arguments from the rate processes. Instead, we create a `stratify_rates` function that takes an existing rate object and stratifies it by additional variables using proportional hazards. This can be used for any stratification variable of the user's choice, so it allows users to quickly build up a stratified rate schedule from an initial schedule.

We also adjusted the `calculate_*_rates` functions to take a single `by` argument as a character vector rather than the various boolean by_* that were used across different functions. This allows more flexibility in how users can stratify the lexis counts they desire and makes it easy to inlude group columns that have unique names.

## Stratifying Rates

```{r}


fertility_rates <- get_fertility_hfd("USA", 2000)
mortality_rates <- get_mortality_hmd("USA", 2000)

fertility_rates <- stratify_rates(
  fertility_rates, 
  by = list(
    group = c(A = 1.1, B = 1),
    # this is not really a great idea for union type as within union
    # type fertility rates have a totally different age profile, but 
    # ok for testing purposes
    union_type = c("unpartnered" = 0.3, "partnered" = 1.3)
  )
)
fertility_rates |> calculate_tfr()

# a better approach is to start with rates pre-stratified by union type and
# then stratify further by group
fertility_rates_by_union_type <- read_csv(
  here(
  "validation", "data", "usa_2000_2001", "usa_2000_fertility_by_union_status.csv"
  )
) |>
  rename(union_type = union_status)
fertility_rates <- stratify_rates(
  fertility_rates_by_union_type,
  by = list(group = c(A = 1.1, B = 1))
)
fertility_rates |> calculate_tfr()

# for a more complicated approach, we can break the proportional hazards assumption
# by stratifying rates by subsets of the rate schedule and then binding back together

fertility_rates <- bind_rows(
  fertility_rates_by_union_type |>
    filter(union_type == "partnered") |>
    stratify_rates(list(group = c(A = 1.05, B = 1))),
  fertility_rates_by_union_type |>
    filter(union_type == "unpartnered") |>
    stratify_rates(list(group = c(A = 1.20, B = 1)))
)
fertility_rates |> calculate_tfr()

mortality_rates <- stratify_rates(
  mortality_rates,
  list(group = c(A = 1.05, B = 1))
)
mortality_rates |>
  calculate_life_table() |>
  filter(age_start == 0) |>
  select(group, sex, ex)
```

```{r}

mar_rates <- read_csv(
  here("validation", "data", "usa_2000_2001", "usa_2001_marriage_rates_female.csv")
)


set.seed(42)
pop_start <- create_baseline_population(50000, group_weights = c(A = 1, B = 1))

model <- hammel_model() |>
  set_population(pop_start) |>
  set_fertility(fertility_rates) |>
  set_mortality(mortality_rates) |>
  set_union_formation("rate", rates = mar_rates)

pop_end <- simulate(model, 150, 42)
```

```{r}

calculate_fertility_rates(pop_end, c(50, 150), seq(15, 45, 5)) |>
  calculate_tfr()

calculate_fertility_rates(pop_end, c(50, 150), seq(15, 45, 5), 
                          by = "group") |>
  calculate_tfr()

calculate_fertility_rates(pop_end, c(50, 150), seq(15, 45, 5), 
                          by = c("group", "union_type")) |>
  calculate_tfr()

calculate_mortality_rates(pop_end, c(50, 150),  0:95, by = "group") |>
  calculate_life_table() |>
  filter(age_start == 0) |>
  select(group, sex, ex)
```





## Unit Tests

The following tests have been constructed and are currently all passing.

```{r}
#| label: test-results
#| eval: true

test_results <- devtools::test(pkg = here::here(), reporter = "silent")
test_table <- as.data.frame(test_results)
knitr::kable(
  test_table[, c("test", "passed", "failed", "error", "skipped", "warning")]
)
```
## Conclusions and Unresolved Limitations

This milestone meets all expectation. The new approach to producing events is working as expected and continues to preserve input rates in the output. The new approach increases runtime slightly in some situations but reduces it in other situations. The weight models are producing the expected proportional hazards in the output.

Remaining limitations include the fact that weights may fail to produce expected difference when bins are sparsely populated and the continued issue of unrealized births in sparse bins.
